title: SAFI Cuts VLA Robot Safety Violations 98% Mid-Task
summary: Notre Dame's SAFI method reduces vision-language-action robot prohibited-task completion from 99.7% to 1.3% after mid-execution takeover, with zero incidents.
body_markdown:
#### 💡 TL;DR


- Notre Dame researchers released SAFI, a training method that stops VLA robots from completing prohibited tasks after mid-execution takeover.
- SAFI reduced prohibited-task completion from 99.7% to 1.3% on LIBERO benchmarks using OpenVLA-OFT, with zero physical incidents recorded.
- The two-stage method labels prohibited demonstrations with stationary arm targets while preserving gripper state, then trains jointly with retained tasks.


University of Notre Dame researchers have published State-Aware Fallback Imitation (SAFI), a two-stage training method that teaches vision-language-action robots to abort prohibited behaviors mid-execution without dropping held objects. On LIBERO benchmarks using OpenVLA-OFT, SAFI reduced successful prohibited-task completion after mid-execution takeover from 99.7% to 1.3%, with zero recorded physical incidents. The method preserves retained-task performance while addressing a critical safety gap that initial-state refusal benchmarks miss.


## Release Date and Availability


Officially released on November 20, 2026, the SAFI method is detailed in the paper "Teaching Vision-Language-Action Models to Stop Safely" by researchers Chuhan Wang, Jinduo Guo, Yue Huang, and Meng Jiang at Notre Dame, with Xiangchi Yuan at Georgia Tech and Ningshan Ma at MIT. The implementation code is published under the repository franciscoliu/SAFI, making the technique immediately accessible to robotics researchers.


## The Mid-Execution Safety Gap


Existing safety benchmarks test whether robots refuse prohibited tasks from their initial state. SAFI targets a more insidious failure mode: policies that suppress a task from its initial state can still complete it when taking over partway through execution. The researchers frame the problem clearly: stopping the task is not enough if the robot drops a held object in the process. "Non-completion is an incomplete measure of safety," they write, pointing to physical incidents as the true risk metric.


Baseline methods illustrate the severity of this gap. NPO-RT records 31.9% Target Success and a 19.9% Physical Incident Rate on LIBERO after mid-execution takeover. GA and GradDiff push target rates lower but hit the controller's clipping bounds, creating action-saturation episodes. The original OpenVLA-OFT policy completes a prohibited task 99.7% of the time under these conditions.


## How SAFI Works


SAFI operates in two stages that address both safety and capability preservation. The first stage, fallback target construction, relabels every state in a prohibited-task demonstration with a stationary arm command and a gripper-preserving target. The instruction is simple: hold what you were holding. The second stage, joint policy adaptation, trains the model on those holding targets together with the original actions of retained tasks, using LoRA on the language-model layers and updating the inherited action head.


This dual-component design is essential. Ablation studies reveal that stripping the retained-task loss collapses permitted-task performance to zero. Removing the fallback supervision lets the robot finish the prohibited task at 99.7% on Spatial and 100.0% on Object benchmarks, with physical incidents returning. Both components must work in concert.


## Benchmark Performance


On LIBERO after mid-execution takeover, SAFI reduces target success from the original policy's 99.7% to 1.3%, with no recorded physical incidents or action-saturation episodes. Retained-task performance remains robust: 96.9% on the Spatial suite and 93.1% on Object tasks. On the BadLIBERO poisoned-object setting, which tests whether a backdoor-implanted policy can be stopped, SAFI records zero on all three endpoints, matching the performance of RMU.


The method demonstrates that safety interventions need not trade off capability. By jointly training on fallback targets and retained actions, SAFI preserves the full operational envelope of the base policy while eliminating the mid-execution failure mode that initial-state benchmarks miss.


## What This Means


SAFI arrives in a dense cluster of robotics safety research, joining 218 stories tracked across the last 90 days that probe the gap between what a VLA refuses on paper and what it does once its gripper is moving. The method provides a training recipe that robotics labs can apply immediately to any vision-language-action model, addressing a failure mode that becomes more critical as these systems move from research environments into real-world deployments. The zero-incident result on both standard and adversarial benchmarks sets a new bar for mid-execution safety in embodied AI.
